paper_title: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Liu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025) are multimodal in what they observe but largely unimodal in how they reason. Although they perceive both visual and textual inputs, their reasoning process is predominantly carried out in autoregressive text tokens (Wei et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024a). This paradigm is effective when relevant visual evidence has been captured, leaving only logical inference to be performed. However, in practice, the perceived visual input can be either incomplete or unfaithful, especially on challenging vision tasks. As an example, Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026c) achieves only 34.7% accuracy on MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2026a), substantially below the 97% human accuracy, while textual reasoning raises the score by only 0.3 points to 35.0%. Such marginal gain from textual reasoning suggests that visual perception remains key bottleneck, constraining what further reasoning can achieve with incomplete or unreliable visual evidence. Several approaches have been explored in prior work to address the perceptual bottleneck. Explicit visual-tool methods zoom, crop, or augment the input, but require external execution and additional visual processing at inference (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026). Unified models combine understanding and generation (Dong et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025b), but generation is rarely used to provide useful feedback for perception or reasoning, direction explored only recently (Li et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026). Latent visual-reasoning methods extend reasoning beyond discrete text tokens to continuous, semantically aligned visual states (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Pham and Ngo, 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Shen and Elhoseiny, 2026), yet non-negligible gap remains between latent semantic alignment and faithful, question-conditioned visual 1 Figure 1 Adaptive multi-modal reasoning with visual imagination. Conventional VLMs perceive multimodal inputs but reason entirely in text. AVTR adaptively harnesses the complementary strengths of visual imagination and textual reasoning according to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Visual imagination forms question-conditioned visual state through visual queries with training-time generative supervision, while requiring no pixel generation at inference. perception. In this work, we present AVTR, which introduces visual imagination as an intermediate step to complement textual reasoning. It encourages the model to revisit relevant visual evidence before generating textual answer, rather than reasoning directly from its initial visual observation. We enable this process by bridging the output from language model to the visual generative space, allowing it to produce visual evidence, which is useful to the task. We further teach the model to distill salient visual evidence through generative visual reflection and leverage it for question-answering tasks. More importantly, the visual generator is solely used as the training-time supervision and is completely removed at inference. Therefore, the model is capable of reasoning from the learned visual states without decoding them into pixels. Furthermore, our empirical analysis reveals that visual imagination and textual reasoning exhibit complementary strengths across different reasoning demands (Figure 3). Visual imagination is particularly effective for improving perception-intensive tasks by distilling task-relevant visual evidence, whereas textual reasoning remains great advantage for explicit relational and compositional inference. This complementarity calls for an adaptive selection of the reasoning route, in way to best preserve answer correctness while avoiding unnecessary computation. To this end, we propose adaptive multimodal reasoning, formulating it as learned routing problem over visual imagination and textual reasoning. shared policy selects direct answering, visual imagination, textual reasoning, or their composition according to the demands of each question. We perform extensive evaluations on various tasks, i.e. high-resolution image understanding, spatial reasoning, video understanding, and temporal grounding over total 16 benchmarks. Across all the benchmarks, AVTR achieves strong average gain over different backbone modes, improving by large margin of 4.9 points over direct answering and by 4.5 points over textual reasoning. In the meantime, we are able to reduce the average inference latency by 33% w.r.t textual reasoning (Figure 6). Note that particularly on 2Bparameter backbone, AVTR achieves significant 6.3 points gain over the reference model. As result, AVTR demonstrates that both visual imagination and adaptive routing improve reasoning quality and efficiency across different model scales. Contributions. Our contributions are summarized in threefold: We introduce visual imagination as an intermediate reasoning modality that revisits visual observations and distills task-relevant evidence for sophisticated vision tasks. We formulate adaptive multi-modal reasoning as learned routing problem over visual imagination and textual reasoning. Such design enables single policy to select or compose the two based on each 2 inputs perceptual and inferential demands. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AVTR on 16 benchmarks spanning diverse reasoning tasks. Our results show consistent improvements in both evaluation metrics and inference efficiency. Meanwhile, it also scales effectively to smaller 2B backbone.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Think with Vision. VLMs combine visual encoders with language models and have achieved strong performance on image and video understanding (Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024a; Tong et al., 2024). Fine-grained visual questions remain challenging because attention can be drawn to visually salient but task-irrelevant tokens (Kang et al., 2025). Existing methods address this by explicitly selecting visual evidence, such as relevant regions or temporal spans, by using tools to crop, zoom, annotate, or re-encode selected regions (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026). While effective, these approaches typically introduce additional visual processing at inference. AVTR instead forms question-conditioned visual state that revisits the original observation and distills task-relevant evidence. Latent Visual Reasoning. Latent reasoning replaces explicit textual traces with continuous states (Hao et al., 2024; Goyal et al., 2024). Recent VLM methods align language-model hidden states with visual features and feed them back as inputs for subsequent reasoning (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Pham and Ngo, 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Shen and Elhoseiny, 2026; Jeon et al., 2026). This output-to-input reuse may introduce representation gap, while autoregressive state generation adds sequential inference cost. In contrast, AVTR inserts learnable visual queries directly into the VLM input and forms question-conditioned visual state in single forward pass through generative visual reflection in latent pixel. Adaptive Reasoning. Recent work has explored adapting textual reasoning to input difficulty. AdaptThink (Zhang et al., 2025) learns to switch between Thinking and NoThinking modes, while VideoAuto-R1 (Liu et al., 2026) uses the confidence of an initial answer to decide whether further reasoning is needed. Other methods adapt textual computation through stopping or inference-time budgets (Chen et al., 2025b; Sui et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025). These approaches only focus on adapting textual reasoning depth. In contrast, AVTR makes reasoning both multimodal and adaptive, allowing the model to select between visual imagination and textual reasoning based on route-level correctness and cost, while separately optimizing reasoning within each route through route-conditioned GRPO.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Given visual input and question q, standard VLM πθ predicts an answer from the visual and textual context. AVTR augments this process with visual imagination, forming question-conditioned visual state that distills task-relevant visual evidence for answer generation. Visual replay first aligns this state with the visual generative space, visual reflection makes it question-dependent, and imagination-guided supervised finetuning teaches the VLM to leverage it for answering. We then learn an outcome-guided adaptive routing policy from the empirical performance of different reasoning routes. The policy adaptively selects among direct answering, visual imagination, textual reasoning, and their composition for each input. Figure 2 gives an overview.

3.1 Visual Imagination Through Replay and Reflection
Visual Replay. As illustrated in Figure 2(a), visual replay first learns a set of visual states that connect the
VLM representation space to a visual generator through reconstruction (Pan et al., 2025). Let Q ∈ Rn×d
denote n learnable visual queries with hidden dimension d. The text prompt p is either the associated image
caption or a general reconstruction instruction, “Please reconstruct this image”. The VLM processes [V; p; Q]
in a single forward pass, and HQ ∈ Rn×d denotes the last hidden states at the query positions. A connector
gψ, parameterized by ψ, maps HQ to the conditioning space of the visual generator vϕ, parameterized by ϕ.

(a) Visual imagination is learned in two stages with shared trainable parameters but different inputs and supervision: visual replay reconstructs the input from visual queries, while visual reflection conditions them on the question to generate relevant visual evidence. (b) Imagination-guided SFT jointly optimizes visual-generation and response objectives, enabling the resulting visual state to guide answer generation. The connector and generator provide training-only supervision and are removed at inference. (c) Adaptive reasoning learns correctnessand cost-aware policy that selects direct answering, visual imagination, textual reasoning, or visual imagination followed by textual reasoning for each input.

Training with these targets encourages HQ to focus on the visual evidence needed to answer the question. Appendix describes target localization, verification, and gain-based filtering.

4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics. We evaluate high-resolution image understanding on V∗ (Wu and
Xie, 2024), HR-Bench-4K/8K (Wang et al., 2025b), and BLINK (Fu et al., 2024); spatial reasoning on
ERQA (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025), MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2026a), VSI-Bench (Yang et al.,
2025a), and RealWorldQA (xAI, 2024); and video understanding on MVBench (Li et al., 2024b), Video-
MME (Fu et al., 2025), LongVideoBench (Wu et al., 2024), and MLVU (Zhou et al., 2025b). These benchmarks
are evaluated using their official accuracy metrics. We further evaluate temporal grounding using mIoU on
Charades-STA (Gao et al., 2017), QVHighlights (Lei et al., 2021), ActivityNet Captions (Krishna et al., 2017),
and NExT-GQA (Xiao et al., 2024). Appendix B provides the baseline sources and complete evaluation
protocol.
sections.content: Implementation Details. We use Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026c,b) as the VLM backbones, with = 64 learnable visual queries and 6-layer connector to SANA-1.6B (Xie et al., 2025a) at 512 512 resolution. Training proceeds in four stages: visual replay on 5M captioned images with the VLM frozen for alignment; visual reflection on 178K question-conditioned targets; SFT on 380K instruction examples; and 6 adaptive routing on 20K questions with = 4 rollouts per route. We set λimag = 0.2 and λgate = 0.02. All models use the same prompts and greedy decoding, with up to 20K visual tokens, 256 video frames sampled at 2 fps, and 8,192 newly generated tokens. Appendix and provide the full training and evaluation details.

4.2 Main Results
Image and spatial understanding. Table 1 shows consistent gains across high-resolution understanding and
spatial reasoning. Relative to direct answering with the backbone (w/o Think), AVTR improves all eight
benchmarks and raises the average from 67.1 to 73.2, a 6.1-point gain. The improvement is particularly
pronounced on spatial reasoning (+8.3 points), with the largest gain on VSI-Bench (+13.8 points). This
pattern is consistent with the intended role of visual imagination: generating task-relevant visual evidence
that supports visual perception and spatial reasoning.

4.3 Visual and Textual Reasoning Are Complementary
Reasoning-mode ablation. Table 4 compares different fixed reasoning routes with adaptive routing. Enabling
visual imagination consistently improves over the direct route, and replacing the learned visual state at

always using visual imagination, textual reasoning, or their composition is inferior to adaptive routing on
average. In particular, simply enabling more reasoning does not guarantee better performance. The benefit
therefore comes from selecting the appropriate reasoning modality for each question rather than applying
a fixed reasoning pattern globally. Table 7 (Appendix) further analyzes activation rates of the visual and
textual gates under the learned adaptive policy for each benchmark.

sections.title: 4.6 Adaptive Reasoning Improves Performance and Efficiency
sections.content: Figure 6 shows that visual imagination improves accuracy with only 0.6 seconds of additional latency. This low overhead follows (i) Visual queries are inserted and from two design choices. processed in parallel rather than generated token by token. (ii) The generator is removed at inference, so answers are conditioned directly on the intermediate visual states without pixel decoding. Adaptive reasoning further selects route for each question and invokes textual reasoning only when needed. In contrast, the backbones fixed textual-reasoning mode generates full reasoning trace for every input. Combining visual and textual reasoning on demand improves the mean score over the 16 benchmarks by 4.5 points while reducing latency by 4.3 seconds. Appendix reports the accuracy, latency, and number of generated tokens of each configuration.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Figure 6 Efficiency analysis. Mean score over the 16 benchmarks versus average latency per query. We proposed AVTR, which introduces visual imagination as complementary reasoning modality and adaptively selects how to reason for each question. Generative visual states revisit task-relevant evidence and directly condition answer generation without pixel decoding at inference. learned routing policy selects or composes visual imagination and textual reasoning according to the perceptual and inferential demands of each input. Experiments on various image and video understanding benchmarks consistently validate the advantages of our model. We further show that the same framework remains effective with Qwen3.5-2B backbone, enabling lightweight adaptive visual-textual reasoning model and highlighting the broader applicability of AVTR across model scales.

sections.title: A Training Data and Optimization
sections.content: The training contains four stages: visual replay, question-conditioned reflection, imagination-guided SFT, and adaptive routing. All phases use bfloat16 precision on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. We report the settings that determine optimization and effective data scale, omitting infrastructure-specific parameters. A.1 Training Schedule Stage-0: Visual Replay. Visual replay is trained on approximately 5M captioned images from BLIP3o-PretrainShort-Caption (Chen et al., 2025a), CC12M (Changpinyo et al., 2021), and InternVL-SA-1B-Caption (Kirillov et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b,a) on 128 A100 GPUs for 50K steps. The Qwen3.5-9B backbone and visual autoencoder are frozen. We optimize the SANA-1.6B generator, 64 visual queries, and 6-layer connector with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), peak learning rate of 3 105, and cosine decay. All targets are reconstructed at 512 512 resolution. Figures 7 and 8 show representative reconstructions, while Table 8 quantifies the effect of the query budget. Figure 7 Visual Reconstruction Quality. Each example shows an input image, its associated image caption, and its reconstruction image. Stage-1: Visual Reflection. Starting from visual replay, we train on approximately 178K question-conditioned targets retained by the pipeline in Appendix C. The targets comprise salient regions for images and salient frames for videos. We retain the same frozen backbone and autoencoder and update only the generator, queries, and connector. Training uses AdamW with learning rate 3 105 for one epoch with 64 A100 GPUs. Stage-2: Imagination-Guided SFT. The SFT mixture contains approximately 380K examples from the sources summarized in Table 6. It combines spatial question answering, general video question answering, and temporal grounding. Target-free examples remain in the mixture and contribute only the response loss. We freeze the generator and visual autoencoder and optimize the VLM, visual queries, and connector for one epoch. We use AdamW with learning rate 106, weight decay 0.1, global batch size of 128, and cosine decay with 3% warmup with 64 A100 GPUs. For datasets that also serve as evaluation benchmarks, we train only on their official training splits and evaluate on held-out splits. 15 Table 6 Training data. The imagination-guided SFT mixture contains approximately 380K image, spatial, and video examples, including 178K data with verified visual target. Type Image Spatial Size 28.2K 191.2K Video 160.5K Details Visual-CoT (Shao et al., 2024a) JoyAI-Image-OpenSpatial (Song et al., 2026) Open-o3-Video (Meng et al., 2025), VideoChat3-LV116K (Li et al., 2026b) ActivityNet Captions (Krishna et al., 2017), Charades-STA (Gao et al., 2017) QVHighlights (Lei et al., 2021), NExT-GQA (Xiao et al., 2024) Stage-3: Adaptive Routing Data and Optimization. We construct the routing dataset from the SFT training pool. We first perform route-complete rollouts for each question and discard samples for which either all four routes are correct or all four are incorrect, as these cases provide no discriminative supervision for route selection. Among questions solved by exactly one route, we balance the four corresponding route categories so that no reasoning mode dominates the routing data. This results in training set of 20K questions. During routing optimization, we force all four routes and sample four rollouts per route for each question. We train with training batch size of 8, learning rate of 4 106, and GRPO clipping coefficients ϵl = ϵh = 0.2. We set the route costs to C(Direct) = 0, C(Visual) = 0.01, C(Textual) = 0.04, and C(Visual+Textual) = 0.05. We set λgate = 0.02 based on the approximate gradient magnitudes of the two objectives, keeping the weighted gate gradient on the same order of magnitude as the GRPO gradient.

sections.title: B Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Baselines. The proprietary baselines are GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025), GPT-5 mini (OpenAI, 2025), and Gemini 2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025). The open foundation models are Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026c,b), InternVL3.5-8B and InternVL3.5-2B (Wang et al., 2025a), Cambrian-S-7B (Yang et al., 2025b), LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B (An et al., 2026), JoyAI-Image-Und (Song et al., 2026), Gemma 4 E2B (Gemma Team et al., 2026), and MiniCPM-V4.6 (OpenBMB, 2026). The video-specialized baselines are Video-R1 (Feng et al., 2025), Time-R1 (Wang et al., 2026b), VITAL (Zhang et al., 2026), VideoChat-R1.5 (Yan et al., 2026), and VideoAuto-R1 (Liu et al., 2026). In the visual-supervision ablation, the variants with no visual supervision and with feature supervision are trained with the same backbone and instruction data. The latent-reasoning comparison includes LVR (Li et al., 2026a), Monet (Wang et al., 2026a), and VisReflect (Shen and Elhoseiny, 2026). The Qwen3.5 rows marked w/o Think and w/ Think use direct answering and the models built-in textual-reasoning mode, respectively. Evaluation. All models are evaluated using the same prompts and greedy decoding. Videos are sampled at 2 fps, with at most 256 frames and 20K visual tokens. We set maximum generation budget of 8,192 new tokens to handle rare cases where textual reasoning fails to terminate. If the model reaches this limit without producing valid final answer, we fall back to the prediction from the same backbone with thinking disabled, rather than scoring an incomplete reasoning trace.

sections.title: C Visual Target Construction and Filtering
sections.content: We construct the reflection targets Vtgt through candidate localization, target verification, and gain-based filtering. The raw pool contains approximately 0.92M image and video question-answer pairs from the full set of data in Table 6. We infer missing targets through model-assisted localization when possible and then verify all targets, yielding approximately 534K examples: 449K images and 84K salient video frames. The final gain-based filter retains approximately 178K examples for reflection training, comprising approximately 155K image targets and 23.5K video targets. These statistics describe the dedicated question-conditioned reflection set. 16 Candidate Localization. For image examples with ground-truth bounding box, we directly use it to crop the image as the target. When bounding box is unavailable, Qwen3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026a) predicts the region that supports the reference answer. For video examples with an annotated temporal span, we sample candidate frame from that span. When temporal span is unavailable, Qwen3.5-27B first localizes the relevant interval, from which we sample the candidate frame. The resulting cropped image or salient frame defines Vtgt. Target Verification. We next ask Qwen3.5-27B to verify each proposed localization against the original visual input, question, and reference answer. target passes verification only when the marked region or sampled frame contains visual evidence that directly supports the reference answer. This stage removes empty, irrelevant, and incorrectly localized targets before they are used for training. Gain-Based Filtering. Verification establishes that target is relevant, but not that it improves the models answer. We therefore evaluate the same base VLM twice. The base model receives the original visual input and question, [V; q], while the target-conditioned run appends the verified target, [V; q; Vtgt]. For multiple-choice and exact-match questions, we retain wrong-to-correct transitions. For temporal grounding, we require positive increase in temporal IoU. This paired criterion ensures that each retained target contributes measurable evidence beyond the original input.

F.2 Complementary Strengths of Visual and Textual Reasoning Task-level comparison. We measure route preference as the accuracy difference between the forced visual and textual routes of the same checkpoint. Figure 3 shows structured continuum rather than uniform advantage for either modality. The seven largest visual margins all involve metric geometry or viewpoint transformation, spanning room size, multi-view reasoning, relative direction, positional relations, object distance, and object size. Art style and visual similarity show smaller but consistent visual advantages. The strongest textual margins occur in scene sequencing, text-referred tracking, high-resolution cross-instance reasoning, moving direction, and spatial-relation tasks. Action localization, trajectory reasoning, egocentric navigation, counting, functional correspondence, state estimation, and action counting also favor textual reasoning more moderately. Overall, visual imagination is most useful when the answer depends on reconstructing continuous geometry, whereas textual reasoning better preserves discrete entities, counts, and ordered state changes. sections.title: G Comparison With Prior Latent Visual Reasoning
sections.content: Prior latent-visual methods differ in both how their states are computed and how those states are supervised. Figure 12(a) reports paired with-versus-without-visual comparison within each method. For AVTR, these settings correspond to the Direct and fixed Visual routes in Table 4. Enabling our visual state improves all four shared benchmarks, by 1.53 points on average. The corresponding mean changes are 0.31, +0.38, and +0.58 for Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR), Monet, and VisReflect. For AVTR, the largest gains occur on HR-Bench-4K (+2.0) and BLINK (+2.6), matching the high-resolution setting for which the state is designed. Figure 12 Generative visual imagination improves both accuracy and efficiency. (a) Accuracy on four high-resolution benchmarks; numbers indicate gains from enabling visual reasoning. (b) Average accuracy over the four benchmarks versus latency. Figure 12(b) places these results against the reported cost of constructing the visual state. AVTR reaches 83.7 average accuracy at 50 ms, compared with 67.0 to 71.5 at 83 to 437 ms for the autoregressive methods. The latency pattern is consistent with the expected advantage of parallel queries over autoregressive latent generation.
